citation: Young, V. M., Humphrey, D. C., Wang, H., Bosetti, K. R., Cassidy, L., Wechsler, M. E., Rivera, E., Murray, S., & Schanzenbach, D. W. (2008). Renaissance Schools Fund-Supported Schools: Early Outcomes, Challenges, and Opportunities. SRI International. https://www.sri.com
title: Promising practices in new schools cluster in five interrelated areas: teacher capacity, data-driven decision-making, continuous instructional improvement, school culture and high expectations, and parent engagement
description: The report's case studies of RSF-supported schools organize promising practices into five areas the authors examined: "The schools’ efforts to build teacher capacity through their hiring, evaluation, and professional development practices," data use at school and classroom levels, continuous curricular and instructional improvement with remediation strategies, school culture and expectations, and parent engagement. Practices were selected for "coherence of combined practices and the depth and intensity (rather than superficiality) of those practices." The report treats these areas as interrelated rather than independent levers.
requirements: Practices were identified in schools still early in development; the report links them to future rather than current test-score gains
constraints: The report states the crucial factor is how schools use structures to strengthen instruction rather than just that the structures are in place
target_learners: K-12 students in new schools of choice in high-need urban communities
target_learning_goals: Accelerated student learning in reading and mathematics during a new school's early years
examples: Case studies across Cohort 1 schools and a subset of Cohort 2 schools over three rounds of site visits
key_sources: Young, V. M., Humphrey, D. C., Wang, H., Bosetti, K. R., Cassidy, L., Wechsler, M. E., Rivera, E., Murray, S., & Schanzenbach, D. W. (2008). Renaissance Schools Fund-Supported Schools: Early Outcomes, Challenges, and Opportunities. SRI International. https://consortium.uchicago.edu/publications/renaissance-schools-fund-supported-schools-early-outcomes-challenges-and-opportunities

article_title: Co-Creating Buildable and Open Social Robot Study Companions with University Students
citation: Farnaz Baksh, Matevž B. Zorec, Feiazie Baksh, and Karl Kruusamäe. (2026). Co-Creating Buildable and Open Social Robot Study Companions with University Students. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.15239v1
title: Robot Study Companion (RSC) v4.1 open-source social robot chassis
description: The RSC is an affordable, compact, 3D-printed desktop social robot built around a Raspberry Pi with peripherals enabling multimodal interaction, including a touchscreen, servo-driven flippers, an LED ring, microphones, and speakers. The v4.1 chassis redesign applies DfA and DfD interventions: a twist-lock chassis replacing internal screws, snap-fit speaker base and front panel, one-way component fits with fiducial markers, print-in-place latches giving tool-free SD/USB access, a bespoke expansion PCB consolidating wiring breakouts, and a rewritten step-by-step guide with synchronised video and text. All open-source artefacts are released at the project site for community contribution.
requirements: Assembly relies on 3D-printed reinforced parts and off-the-shelf electronics; the rewritten documentation guide at the project site supports the build.
constraints: The v4.1 documentation was deliberately kept in an alpha state during evaluation, and the designations v4 and v4.1 refer specifically to the chassis mechanical design, not electronics or software tracks.
target_learners: university students facing isolation and motivational challenges
first-time robot builders in Guyana and Estonia
target_learning_goals: constructionist hands-on learning through building a social robot
technical agency and emotional support via a physical companion
examples: Two replication cases (Guyana capstone students, an Estonia one-day workshop) informed the v4 to v4.1 transition, and Studies 1 and 2 evaluated the redesigned chassis.
key_sources: Farnaz Baksh, Matevž B. Zorec, Feiazie Baksh, and Karl Kruusamäe. (2026). Co-Creating Buildable and Open Social Robot Study Companions with University Students. https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.15239

article_title: Cognitive flexibility in adolescence: Neural and behavioral mechanisms of reward prediction error processing in adaptive decision making during development
citation: Hauser, T. U., Iannaccone, R., Walitza, S., Brandeis, D., & Brem, S. (2015). Cognitive flexibility in adolescence: Neural and behavioral mechanisms of reward prediction error processing in adaptive decision making during development. Neuroimage, 104, 347-354. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neuroimage.2014.09.018
title: Risk-sensitive reinforcement learning model with anticorrelated valuation (RSAV) for reversal learning
description: The RSAV model is a reinforcement learning model in which chosen and unchosen stimulus values are anticorrelated: feedback about the chosen object also informs the value of the unchosen stimulus, and separate learning rates are kept for positive and negative RPEs (αChosen+/−, αUnchosen+/−). The article states that "in reversal learning tasks, the feedback about the chosen object also informs about the value of the unchosen stimulus", and implements the anticorrelation within a risk-sensitive model following Niv et al. (2012), where individual risk sensitivity is assessed by using different learning rates for positive and negative RPEs. Action probabilities are derived with a softmax selection function, and parameters are estimated by maximum log-likelihood with a genetic search algorithm.
requirements: Feedback-based learning in which reward contingencies reverse unpredictably, so that feedback on the chosen option carries information about the unchosen option
Estimation of separate learning-rate parameters for positive and negative prediction errors via maximum-likelihood fitting
constraints: The article notes it was previously shown that models with anticorrelated valuation fit this task better than a standard Rescorla-Wagner model, i.e., the model is tailored to probabilistic reversal learning rather than all learning tasks
target_learning_goals: cognitive flexibility in detecting changes in reward contingencies
examples: Fitted to trial-by-trial choices of 19 adolescents and 17 adults performing a probabilistic reversal learning task with 80%/20% reward probabilities and reversals after at least 6 correct choices
key_sources: Hauser, T. U., Iannaccone, R., Walitza, S., Brandeis, D., & Brem, S. (2015). Cognitive flexibility in adolescence: Neural and behavioral mechanisms of reward prediction error processing in adaptive decision making during development. Neuroimage, 104, 347-354. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.neuroimage.2014.09.018

article_title: Measuring strategy use with self-report instruments: theoretical and empirical considerations
citation: Gonny Schellings & Bernadette Van Hout-Wolters. (2011). Measuring strategy use with self-report instruments: theoretical and empirical considerations. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-011-9081-9
title: RSAT: a computer-based on-line reading assessment measuring comprehension and spontaneous reading strategies
description: RSAT is a computer-based reading assessment designed to measure readers' comprehension and spontaneous use of reading strategies while reading texts. Readers comprehend passages one sentence at a time and answer an indirect self-report question about their understanding of each target sentence, or a direct comprehension question such as "Why X?". Answers are digitally analyzed by counting target words associated with strategies or comprehension, and the resulting measures are used to predict comprehension scores on standardized tests.
requirements: Digital analysis counting target words associated with strategies or comprehension
constraints: It is an on-line instrument, in contrast to the retrospective off-line questionnaires used in the first two special-issue contributions
target_learning_goals: reading comprehension and spontaneous reading strategy use
examples: Magliano, Millis, the RSAT Development Team, Levinstein and Boonthum examine this on-line instrument in the third special-issue contribution
key_sources: Gonny Schellings & Bernadette Van Hout-Wolters. (2011). Measuring strategy use with self-report instruments: theoretical and empirical considerations. Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-011-9081-9

article_title: Effectiveness of relationships and sex education: A systematic review of terminology, content, pedagogy, and outcomes
citation: van Leent, Lisa, Walsh, Kerryann, Moran, Claire, Hand, Kirstine, & French, Sally (2023). Effectiveness of relationships and sex education: A systematic review of terminology, content, pedagogy, and outcomes. Educational Research Review, 39, Article number: 100527. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2023.100527
title: A taxonomy of terminology for school-based relationships and sexuality education
description: The review presents a taxonomy of the terms used to describe school-based relationships and sexuality education, identifying terms including "sexuality education, sex education, holistic sexuality education, sexual and reproductive health, relationships and sex education, sexual health/education, comprehensive sex/sexual education/health education". It charts how often each term was defined and which sources (UNESCO, SIECUS, WHO, IPPF, author-defined) supplied definitions, concluding the terms used in the field are vast and inconsistently defined.
requirements: Studies must report the term used and a definition for the taxonomy to classify them
constraints: Applies to universal school-based RSE for children aged 4-18 published in English 2000-2020; excludes targeted cohorts and abstinence-only approaches
examples: The most frequently-defined term was sexuality education, defined in 9 of 33 clearly defined papers, drawing variously on UNESCO, SIECUS, and author-defined sources
key_sources: van Leent, Lisa, Walsh, Kerryann, Moran, Claire, Hand, Kirstine, & French, Sally (2023). Effectiveness of relationships and sex education: A systematic review of terminology, content, pedagogy, and outcomes. Educational Research Review, 39, Article number: 100527. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2023.100527

article_title: Effectiveness of relationships and sex education: A systematic review of terminology, content, pedagogy, and outcomes
citation: van Leent, Lisa, Walsh, Kerryann, Moran, Claire, Hand, Kirstine, & French, Sally (2023). Effectiveness of relationships and sex education: A systematic review of terminology, content, pedagogy, and outcomes. Educational Research Review, 39, Article number: 100527. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2023.100527
title: A taxonomy of teaching approaches used to deliver school-based RSE
description: The review classifies the pedagogical approaches reported in RSE studies into categories including multiple strategies, health promotion, delivery personnel, a suite of active learning pedagogies, cross-curriculum approaches, UNESCO guidance, philosophy/ethics, and sex/gender-based approaches. It reports a "striking lack of standardised use of pedagogical terms" and that detail explaining the approaches used was starkly missing, hindering replication and further testing.
requirements: Studies must describe their program approach for classification; the review argues reporting guidelines for RSE studies are needed
constraints: Only 38 of 134 studies provided approach information; 66 provided none
examples: Four studies espoused active learning pedagogies incorporating role-play, discussion, demonstrations, simulations and games; 11 studies used multiple strategies

article_title: A comparative study of nurses' competencies in integrating religion/spirituality into patient care.
citation: Farokhzadian Jamileh, Sabzi Amirreza, Farmitani Zakieh. (2025). A comparative study of nurses’ competencies in integrating religion/spirituality into patient care. BMC Health Services Research. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12913-025-12613-z
title: Religious/Spiritually Integrated Practice Assessment Scale (RSIPAS)
description: The RSIPAS is a 40-item self-report instrument, developed and validated by Oxhandler et al. in the United States, measuring nurses' competencies in integrating clients' religion/spirituality into practice. It has four subscales — self-efficacy, attitudes, perceived feasibility, and behaviors — rated on 5-point Likert scales, with total scores from 40 to 200. This study used it to compare competencies across two hospital types, with scores of 94–146 classified as "moderate competence". Reliability in the Persian version reached Cronbach's alpha of 91.2 for the overall scale.
requirements: Requires nurses with a bachelor's degree or higher and at least six months of work experience in the studied hospitals, as applied in this study's inclusion criteria
constraints: The authors note the self-administered tool "may not fully capture the complex nature of integrating patients’ religion/spirituality into practice"
target_learners: Practicing nurses in general and psychiatric hospitals
target_learning_goals: Assessing and integrating patients' religion/spirituality into clinical nursing practice
examples: Used in 2023 with 200 Iranian nurses via self-administered face-to-face forms taking approximately 18 minutes to complete
key_sources: Farokhzadian Jamileh, Sabzi Amirreza, Farmitani Zakieh. (2025). A comparative study of nurses’ competencies in integrating religion/spirituality into patient care. BMC Health Services Research. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12913-025-12613-z
